Chess. En passant capture. Yes, real chess players know this but when playing casual chess most people are completely unaware.

En passant is a move in chess. It is a special pawn capture, that can only occur immediately after a pawn moves two ranks forward from its starting position and an enemy pawn could have captured it had the pawn moved only one square forward. Note that the capturing pawn must be on its fifth rank prior to executing this maneuver. The opponent captures the just-moved pawn "as it passes" through the first square. The resulting position is the same as if the pawn had moved only one square forward and the enemy pawn had captured it normally.

Part of my job is interacting with customers and resolving some issues. Normally, I have a legalistic and authoritative personality, so if someone doesn’t respect the protocol set in place to help resolve these issues (for getting a refund, for example), then I generally reject the request and explain why their refund goes against policy.

Generally, my leniency is dependent on how I judge their intention; if they only missed something during the process, then I would excuse it, but if they incompetently ignored the refund process’ regulations and expected foot-washing, then I would reject it.

My question is if it should matter whether or not they were kind throughout the process. Does their rudeness make their refund request any more right or wrong? I have my own bias, so sometimes, I wonder if some of the decisions I make were really justified.

Depends how much leeway you have in the process. If you're allowed to use your discretion for customer satisfaction purposes or otherwise, then absolutely. If someone uses their discretion in how they interact with you to make your life miserable, then why should you use your discretion to make them happy? Someone who walks in being a dick probably wouldn't be satisfied anyways even if you bend over backwards.

Basically, yeah, I am allowed to use my discretion to give leeway to whoever I choose. Customers usually only have several seconds to make their impression, but if they act like they’re above the policy, then I almost always reject the request no matter what else they say.

I’m also generally unsympathetic to emotions when it comes to decision-making, so it’s also common for me to reject requests by people who outright ignored the policy and give me their sob story in hopes that I’m a pushover. When it’s made clear that they do understand the policy but came in anyway thinking that they could guilt trip me, I group them with the rude ones. I think sometimes they do it unintentionally since it’s common to pander to customers.

I don't have an absolute answer but a guideline that I belief you can use to help you think about the dilemma: how would you like to be treated if you were the customer? How would you like to be treated if you were a kind customer? What about an unkind one?

Usually I try to think of things in that way, but this for this situation, it just doesn’t work. I generally make decisions on what I consider sound logic and truth (side effect: arrogance and stubbornness), and almost always disregard emotional things altogether. For example, if I were in the situation that I broke policy and I was made clear I did, with sufficient evidence, I would immediately apologize and dismiss myself and leave. At that point, I would not care if I was given a refund at all, since I naturally prefer truth over how I feel.

Consequently, I have little idea how others would feel in these situations. Based off of the little I know, I believe it is the right thing to award the kind and reject the unkind. In the interest of the devil's advocate, I have asked anyway.

I guess that if you already have this level of understanding it will be hard to help you without knowing more details. You could try basing yourself on other ethical frameworks but that is easier said than done.

One example is Aristotle's golden mean. It's a complex idea but the basic version is that you try to identify extreme opposite behaviors (for example, when you're absolutely certain a person is conning you and when you're absolutely certain the person is being sincere). With those two in mind you try to ascertain what would be the "middle point" between them. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_mean_%28philosophy%29

On a societal level, we can teach people the proper way to act in any given situation. If we reward kindness and conscientious thought then people will tend to move that way in general. If we tell everyone that the customer is always right even (or especially) if they're being a dick or that everyone is a special snowflake who deserves every little concession then we tend to get a self important society that has less of a conscious.

I will generally act in a professional and kindly manner in life, but will absolutely go out of my way to fuck with people who are being assholes. Professionally and personally.
